name: Anti-fashion

lead: Anti-fashion is an umbrella term for dress that is explicitly contrary to the fashion of the day. It can come from indifference to trends, political aims or practicality, and people use it to craft an individual look that does not depend on seasonal cycles.
Examples run from 19th-century dress reform and the Bloomer costume to punk, grunge, 1990s minimalism and avant-garde designers such as Rei Kawakubo and Yohji Yamamoto.

paras: In practice people choose timeless, utilitarian, deconstructed or subcultural pieces over trend-led items. Wikipedia notes that once mainstream retail adopts such styles, they lose their edge.
No physical risks are documented. Commentators note that anti-fashion is often commodified by the industry it opposes.

angle.text: Clothing is one of the most changeable parts of appearance. Anti-fashion offers a defined style direction, from workwear and uniforms to black minimalism, that people adopt for a distinctive look.

lead: Anti-fashion is dress explicitly contrary to the fashion of the day, whether through indifference to fashion, political aims or practicality.[1] Scholars treat it as radical creativity, and note that when mainstream media and retail take up its styles they lose their edge.[1]

For appearance, it is a way to develop a signature look: timeless, utilitarian or subcultural clothing that does not rely on what is currently trending. Grokipedia describes it as stressing nonconformity, anti-commercialism and symbolic resistance, though that source is AI-generated and may contain errors.[2]

Wikipedia traces it from 18th and 19th-century health-driven dress reform through Coco Chanel's "poor girl" style, 1950s jeans and T-shirts, 1970s punk, grunge and 1990s minimalism, and to designers such as Rei Kawakubo, Yohji Yamamoto, Ann Demeulemeester, Martin Margiela and Raf Simons.[1]
infobox: Kawakubo, Yamamoto, Demeulemeester, Margiela, Simons, Westwood[1]

paras: Wikipedia defines anti-fashion as dress explicitly contrary to current fashion, which may reflect indifference to fashion or serve political or practical goals.[1] Grokipedia cites Ted Polhemus and Georg Simmel's 1904 analysis of fashion as framing, though that is unverified AI-generated text.[2]

In the 18th century a minority of women pushed for practical dress for health reasons; in the 1850s the Dress Reform Association in Seneca Falls, New York promoted the Bloomer costume.[1] Early in the 20th century Coco Chanel promoted a "poor girl" style.[1]

In the 1950s young women adopted jeans, plaid shirts, T-shirts and military surplus; punk emerged in 1970s Britain through Vivienne Westwood and Malcolm McLaren; grunge followed in the late 1980s and a minimalist black-and-white look appeared in the 1990s.[1] Japanese designers such as Rei Kawakubo (her 1982 looks nicknamed the "beggar's outfit"), Issey Miyake and Yohji Yamamoto, and Maison Martin Margiela's 1992 Salvation Army collection, are cited examples.[1]

Samantha Holland noted that many feminist women who dress against norms reject the label because of its confrontational tone.[1] Harriet Worsley argued punk showed how fashion could challenge stereotypes of gender and beauty.[1]
